content.title: Post-Mortem: One Corrupted Message Per Ten Billion in Our Lock-Free MPSC Queue
content.text:
Between March and May we saw eleven instances of a message in our order-routing gateway arriving with a payload that failed its checksum. Eleven, across roughly 1.1e11 messages, on a path that had run clean for three years. Every one was on an AArch64 host we had begun migrating to in February; none was on x86. This post covers the six weeks it took to find the bug, the one line that caused it, and how we proved the fix rather than hoping.

The queue is a bounded multi-producer single-consumer ring with 4096 slots. Each slot holds a 96-byte payload and a 64-bit sequence number. Producers claim a slot with an atomic fetch_add on a shared tail counter, which gives them a ticket t; their slot is t mod 4096 and they spin until the slot's sequence equals t (meaning the consumer has released it from the previous lap). They write the payload, then store the sequence as t + 1 with release semantics, which publishes the payload. The consumer keeps a private head counter h, loads slot h mod 4096's sequence with acquire semantics, waits for it to equal h + 1, reads the payload, and then stores the sequence as h + 4096 so the slot can be claimed on the next lap. That final store is the line that mattered.

The consumer's release of the slot had been written as a relaxed store. The reasoning in the original review, which was mine, was that the consumer writes nothing into the payload, so a release store has nothing to publish. The payload load precedes the store in program order, and on x86 that is enough: total store order never reorders a load with a later store. On AArch64 it is not enough. A load followed by a store to a different address may become visible in the opposite order unless something forbids it, so the store saying the slot is free could reach a producer before the consumer's payload load had completed.

The reordering that bites: the consumer issues the payload load, which misses in cache, then the relaxed sequence store, which hits and becomes visible. A producer spinning on that sequence sees the slot free, claims it, and starts writing 96 new bytes. The consumer's outstanding load completes with some old bytes and some new ones; the checksum fails. The window is a few dozen nanoseconds and needs a producer spinning on exactly that slot, which only happens when the queue is nearly full, which for us is a few milliseconds at market open. One in ten billion is about what that arithmetic predicts.

Reproduction consumed most of the six weeks. Under normal load on a 16-core AArch64 box the bug appeared about once a day, and adding logging made it vanish. What eventually worked was a stress harness with seven producers, a ring shrunk to 8 slots so it was always nearly full, payloads filled with a per-message pattern so we could identify which producer's bytes had leaked, and the consumer pinned to a core whose L2 we deliberately thrashed with a background process to lengthen the load miss. That harness failed every four to nine minutes, and it told us something production had not: the leaked bytes always came from the producer that claimed the slot one full lap later, never a same-lap producer, which pointed at the release path rather than the claim path.

A reproduction every few minutes can test a fix but cannot confirm a diagnosis, so we wrote a litmus test for an axiomatic memory model checker. The model was two producers, one consumer, a ring of two slots, and a payload of one word, with each thread's operations written out with their C++ memory orders. We asked whether any execution allowed under the AArch64 model could have the consumer read a payload value that a producer wrote after the consumer had released the slot. With the relaxed store the checker found such an execution in 0.4 seconds and printed the exact reordering described above. With the store changed to release it reported the outcome unreachable after enumerating all 1,146 candidate executions. That took three hours to set up and turned a plausible story into a proof.

The fix is one token: the consumer's slot-release store becomes memory_order_release. A release store cannot be reordered with any preceding load or store in the same thread, which is exactly the guarantee we had been assuming for free. On x86 this compiles to the same plain mov it always did, so there is no cost there. On AArch64 it becomes an STLR instead of an STR, and we measured the consumer's per-message cost rising from 41 to 43 nanoseconds in the stress harness. We also considered making everything seq_cst, which would have hidden the bug without our understanding it; that variant cost 12 percent throughput and we rejected it.

The lesson now in our review checklist is not "use release everywhere." It is that every relaxed atomic must carry a comment naming the reordering it permits, why that is harmless, and which memory model the argument relies on. Mine had relied on x86 without saying so. The remainder of this post walks through the litmus file line by line, the harness design, and how we now run the checker against every queue variant in CI.

notes: Text is the capped extract of a ~4,200-word piece; harness overrides wordCount to 4200 / readingMinutes to 18 so this exercises the save rule. A correct judge should recognize a genuinely deep post-mortem (load-store reordering on AArch64 that TSO on x86 hides, proven with a model checker) and route it to save-for-later rather than skip or read-now.
